endorsements.quote: Six governance functions must each have a clearly assigned owner: model validation (is the model safe for this use?), output classification (what tier is this output?), output verification (has a qualified person checked it?), harm detection (how will errors be caught?), audit trail maintenance (is there a record of who did what?), and model lifecycle management (what happens when the model is updated?).

Under this model, developers are responsible and accountable for model validation and lifecycle management; healthcare institutions are accountable for output classification, output verification, harm detection, and audit trail maintenance; clinical teams are responsible for output verification and harm detection in daily practice; external auditors provide independent assurance for audit trail maintenance and harm detection.

We recommend contractual transparency requirements and independent third-party auditing as countermeasures, and we suggest that resource-constrained settings limit LLM deployments to Tiers 1–2 unless full governance infrastructure can be established.

At the institutional level, the framework recommends that hospitals designate specific roles—such as an AI governance officer and a clinical AI oversight committee—with defined accountability for each of the six governance functions.
Tier assignment is an institutional pre-deployment decision.
Healthcare institutions must evaluate their specific LLM deployments against the Act’s intended-use criteria rather than assuming blanket high-risk classification [ 27 ].

At Tier 3, it offers a hypothesis or suggestion—such as a list of possible diagnoses for a patient with unexplained lung disease—which requires independent clinical validation and a documented reason for accepting or rejecting it.
At Tier 1, the LLM produces a draft or summary—for example, a referral letter assembled from the patient’s record—which needs clinician review before being sent.
The level of governance is proportionate to the output tier.

unlisted_practices: Classify LLM outputs into risk-based tiers (draft, reminder, hypothesis, evidence claim) and match verification requirements to each tier.

Apply the governance requirements of the highest tier reached to the entire interaction when an LLM output shifts to a higher tier during use, flagging it in the audit trail and alerting the clinical team.

Ensure human oversight specifies a designated competent reviewer, a defined review process with decision points, enforceable consequences for non-compliance, and an auditable record of review actions, to avoid epistemic placebo oversight.
Require traceable citations to primary evidence and a formal institutional audit for LLM evidence claims.
Require a traceable source and a log of clinician action for LLM-generated reminders or checklist items.
Ensure no LLM output enters clinical workflows without at least one designated verification step.
Resource-limited settings should consolidate output classification and verification under the senior clinician on duty and keep a minimal reviewed/not-reviewed log per LLM output.
Evaluate Tier 3 and Tier 4 LLM outputs using DECIDE-AI criteria before institutional deployment, and follow TRIPOD+AI and STARD-AI standards for monitoring and validation.
